He's going to play a lot of special teams for the Arizona Cardinals. He's so effective at it. Um he's played a lot of football at Iowa and in Big 10 football. So he's seen a lot of uh offenses and he's seen a lot of uh different skill positions uh in college. And so he he's adept at that. He he can make tackles. Wilson coming back off of injury, but that other position, there's going to be some healthy competition there, and I think Shy can throw his hat in that ring. >> Rob, you've experienced this whirlwind of draft picks. you pack up and you move and and you're having to learn the playbook, get acclimated, try to make the team. What's number one priority for rookies to set themselves up for success during this time? >> Avoid all distractions. That is the number one priority for for rookies to be successful in the NFL. Anything distraction-wise, tickets, um you know, people, family members, uh friends calling in trying to get you to do things. No, you got to you got to eliminate that and you got to focus in on what's really important and that's being a better football player. >> Being a better football player trying to make this Arizona Cardinals roster. title: The Panthers Huddle: Draft Recap with Dan Morgan and Robert Hunt | Carolina Panthers
text: The following is an exclusive presentation of the Carolina Panthers and the National Football League. On this special episode of the Panthers Huddle, get to know the 2026 Panthers draft class. Plus, we sit down with GM Dan Morgan in the very room where all the big decisions were made. and big game Bobby is here. Robert Hunt drops by the studio to chat with Kristen and TD. Welcome inside the Panthers Huddle. >> Let's go. >> Hey everyone, we're so happy that you join us for this special edition of the Panthers Huddle. Kristen Baloni alongside my co-host and Panthers legend Thomas Davis. TD, let's start with this draft. Now, I thought it was a good draft, but what did you think about it overall? >> I loved it after the fact. So, this is one of those drafts where you you see the names get called, you see the guys that we picked and it's like, wait, what? And then you go back and you see it in totality and it's like, >> when you say, wait, what what did you mean by that? >> Like, we didn't need that guy. We had this guy that we could have used or we could have used this guy. But then when you start thinking about the way that this team has been built, you start thinking about the mindset of Dan Morgan and how he wants this team to operate in his winning in the trenches. And that was a great indicator in this draft that Dan mind is still locked in on bringing dogs in like he talked about and bringing guys in that can contribute upfront so that we can dominate in the trenches. >> Yeah, we love to see that, don't we? I'm going to be talking to Dan Morgan about getting some of those dogs in just a little bit. Very excited for that. All right, though I have to say first round pick, Monroe Freeling out of Georgia tackle. And I tell you what, as soon as they announced that pick, my first thought was TD has to be so happy right now. And look, nobody knows Georgia as well as you do. So tell me about this guy. >> Listen, Marro Freeland is a guy he had to sit and wait his turn. Georgia has had a slew of guys that have been in the rotation that have gone and got drafted. We know that they drafted a lot of guys, but Murro Freeland is a guy that has learned. He's gotten better every single year that he's been at Georgia and he has so much upside. Look at the 9.9 RAW score. That's out of 10 KB. So, it don't get too much better than that. So, that just really shows you just how athletic this kid is. And to me, >> it it's like another Jordan Gross. If he can reach that Jordan Gross potential, then we got a perennial AllPro. We got a guy that I know is going to be special for us for a very long time. And I believe that Monroe Freeland have has that kind of athleticism to get that done. >> Well, you were talking about that score. I was looking at 67315. That's a grown man. What does that do when you have a guy like that out there? And like you said, he's athletic, too. >> Listen, long arms. He's athletic. He's capable of keeping guys off of his quarterback. And no better indicator than that, him at Georgia only giving up one sack over his college career. So, I think that's a huge indicator of what kind of player we're getting. Not only did he get to compete against some of the best guys in practice, he gets to go against some of the best guys on Saturday, playing against guys in the SEC, and he's going to have that same opportunity playing at left tackle, playing in the NFL, and I know without a doubt he's going to be up for the challenge. >> I want to talk about the second round pick now, Lee Hunter. Panthers traded up two spots just to make sure they could get him. What do you see from him? Listen, a big big body man and a guy that can come in and help DB out. I talked about it earlier in the year. We lost one of our big guys. So, we made sure that we added that weight back to that line because at the end of the day, you got to have guys that can keep your linebackers clean. We we brought in some marquee free agents at linebackers. So, we got to make sure that those guys are able to stay clean. And what better way to do it than putting big bodies in front of them? And Lee the fridge hunter is a big body KB. You don't come away with a nickname the fridge and not be a big man. >> No, you're not the toaster or anything like that. And I love that, you know, because we traded up two spots for him. He said, you can see it right there. He said, "I'm ready to run through a brick wall for them." A little bit different the way he said it, but he said that meant so much to him that they wanted him that badly that they were going to make sure that they didn't lose him. KB for any player once you see a team invest that kind of draft capital when they say and I know it wasn't a ton given up but there was something given up to move up for a team to say hey you know what we have this much confidence and and value in you that we're going to give up a a spot or a round in the draft to move up to make sure that we're able to take you so nobody else steals you. So, as a player, you are extremely confident and you walk away knowing that this team absolutely wanted me. It wasn't a situation where I just fell to them. >> And and look, you last year, you famously predicted Tedo McMillan when we thought they were going to go defense in the first round. And this year on the draft show, you came out and you said they need a wide body. And we got I mean, the fridge. >> Dan. Dan, I'm starting to think that you're listening to me. So, I'm just gonna start throwing things out there and see what kind of happened. KB, because at the end of the day, you start saying certain things. We never really know what's going to happen. Talked about T-Mac. We went out and we got him. And we saw how that played out. Offensive rookie of the year. And now, let's see if we can predict this and get big boy a defensive player of the year type rookie of the year type deal. Let's see. >> I love it. I love it. And they're calling you Nostra Thomas here. behind the scenes. All right, we have got plenty more draft coverage coming your way, so stay with us. >> Coming up, Dan Morgan joins Kristen Belone for an exclusive interview from Inside the Draft Room on the Panthers Huddle. This exclusive presentation of the Carolina Panthers Television Network is brought to you in part by Bank of America, the official bank of the Carolina Panthers. Well, >> awesome. Hey, have fun. Enjoy this time with your this moment with your family and your friends. >> I will. I will. Well, thank you guys. >> All right, brother. >> All right. Love you. >> Love you, too. >> Congrats, man. >> So excited now to be joined by Panthers GM Dan Morgan. Dan, we just saw what was my favorite moment of the draft, which is Monroe Freeling saying, "I love you." at the end of his call. What was your reaction to that? Um, I didn't hear him say it at first, but then once I figured out that he said, "I love you," I was like, "Did he just say I love you?" >> So, yeah, it was it was funny. He's got a great personality, great kid, so we're lucky to have him. >> Yeah, it was great to see him in the building. Definitely. Yeah. And as he's going to be a part of this team. This is the second straight year that Pro Football Focus has rated the draft an A+. I remember talking to you about it last year. I know that's not something that you are concerned about, but what I'm wondering is what do you rate this draft? Um, you know, I think, uh, we walked out of the draft really happy. Uh, we we got the guys that we targeted. >> Um, obviously, you're not going to hit on every pick that you, you know, you think you're going to get at the time, but we feel really good about the guys that we got. >> Not only great players, but great culture fits for us and and what we're about here. So, thought it went really good. >> Is it safe to say that the draft board fell the way you wanted it to? Yeah, it did. I think at every pick we we got our guy that was, you know, best available player at the time. So, you know, that's what we want to do here. We want to build the board uh to where we're able to take the best player available at the time. And I think as long as we stick with that, you know, I think things always work out. >> Speaking of uh best player available at the time, in the second round, you traded up two picks to get Lee Hunter. Can you talk to me uh about why that was? >> Yeah. So, sitting there, you know, Lee was kind of standing out there up in the second round and I was just concerned that maybe somebody would jump us and get him, even though it was two picks above us. I was a little nervous. So, I'm like, "Hey, let's just go get our guy. Let's guarantee that we get our guy." And, uh, that's why we jumped up. and I saw his postgame press conference where he was just over the moon that you know that they came up, you know, in two picks just to just to have me and the bond that that creates. Was there a moment on the other side of things where patience paid off and maybe you got someone that that you didn't think would be there? >> Yeah, I mean, you know, I think you can talk about uh Zaki Wheatley, Sam Heck, two guys that we thought really highly of. We thought they'd be gone by the time that we picked them. And you know, we were lucky that they were there. And we were actually surprised that they were there, too, because they were two guys that we thought were really good players and some of the top players at their position. So, uh, for us to be able to get them at the value that we got them, I thought it worked out really well. >> Speaking of them, I'm going to give you all of the guys that you drafted, and I'm hoping that you can give me one or two words to describe each of them. So, of course, starting with Monroe Freeling. Uh, you want just a couple words? I got a lot of words. Absolutely. I mean, obviously he's huge. You know, he's big, he's long, he's athletic. >> Um, and I think he's everything you want in a tackle in the league, you know, to have that size and athleticism. Um, it's hard to find. So, we're lucky to have him. >> We just talked about him. Lee Hunter. >> Yeah. I think with him, he's just a big physical guy. Um, he plays the way that we want our DTackles to play. He plays violent. He's tough. He's strong at the point of attack. So, uh, just another guy that is going to add value to us. >> Yeah, the fridge. >> Yeah. Um, but you know, I just kept trusting the process, trusting the people I love, and, you know, trying to gain knowledge everywhere I was. And, you know, I just kept getting confident, more and more confident in my abilities as I kept getting older and wiser. And, uh, yeah, I'm super happy to be here. Yeah. >> The opportunity to ask this to Daltton, but not to you. Just what it's like for you two to be reunited here on the NFL level. >> Yeah. Um, it's honestly like a dream come true. I mean, I couldn't have imagined, you know, coming to a uh, you know, reaching this this point in my career and getting to do it with my best friend in the world. So, um, you know, it's like we were coming into this brand new thing, you know, joining a brand new team, but I'm doing it with, you know, my closest friend in the world. And it's it was a surreal moment, you know, when when they picked him and um you know, we were screaming on the phone together. So, it's we're super happy to be here. We're we're ready to get to work. >> How big is that for as far as communication on the field as well because you guys know each other so well. >> Yeah, 100%. Yeah. I mean, we got to a point, you know, playing at Arizona where I didn't even have to say anything. You know, we we had been in the same defense for a couple years and I could just look over and know he knows exactly what I'm talking about. So, um you know, now we're we're speaking a different language. Um, but it's football at the end of the day and I know exactly how he operates and, you know, we've been we've been sitting in each other's hotel rooms going over the, you know, over the tape and stuff. So, um, you know, we going to get it right and we going to make sure that that we bring our best um, every every day. >> You had talked about that too. The first call was just kind of like kind of freaked out like this is crazy. What was the first like real conversation like when you guys said, "Oh, this is real. Like we're actually going to do this." >> Yeah. I mean, so yeah. I mean, his first call, um, you know, I was I honestly spent the whole call just screaming on the phone, like I'm JUST SCREAMING, "NO WAY. No way." Um, cuz I was just fre I just couldn't believe it. Like, you know, and then, um, so yeah, when we got on the phone the next day, um, just really like, you know, the day had calmed down a little bit. It was just we just couldn't we still like it was still like a shocking moment like it, but you know, super thankful. You know, the Lord works in in mysterious ways and, you know, he was working his magic on this one. So, um, yeah, it was it was really really cool. >> We heard you have a different locker mate though from Ando that said, uh, he's next to you, getting to know you. What have been your impressions of him? What's he been like out of the gate? >> He is a super funny guy. Um, I been it has been so much fun sitting next to him in the locker room. I only been there for what, like three days or something like that, but no, it's been super cool getting to know him. Um, I'm I'm super excited to get to be his teammate. I I love the way he attacks his work and, you know, he's he's a cool guy off the field, too. So, uh, super cool. >> Played in a pretty unique defense at Arizona under Coach Gonzalez. I'm just curious about what was it in your role in that defense, you know, do you think helped prepare you for the league and kind of what's going to be asked of you? >> Yeah. Um, Coach G, you know, he works in pretty much all different coverages. Um, so I got the chance to to kind of play some safety, play some nickel, um, you know, play some middle field safety, um, in in all type of different ways and, you know, different looks. Um, so I, you know, I got to learn, you know, defensive concepts and instead of just, you know, what do I do in this play and playing a memory game. So, um, being under coach G and and coach RC and those guys, um, you know, they taught us a lot about schemes and how how the defenses work and how how you fit into that to that scheme. So, um, it's it's definitely been helpful um, taking this step here. Um, so I understand what's going on, what we're trying to accomplish and and understanding my role within it. about you playing both safety and nickel today out there on the field. Has the coaching staff indicated to you that they want to use you and kind of like a versatile role playing both back deep and kind of up near the line of scrimmage? >> Yeah. Um that's I mean that's a that's obviously a question that's better suited for them. But um you know I'm going to learn them both um and wherever I can fit best and help the team win some games that's what I'm going to do. Yesterday I was talking to >> you were known for your high character and leadership. How does that translate to this level? >> Yeah. Um I think uh building building a great team starts with being a great teammate first. Um and that's something I learned the importance of um throughout my entire football career honestly. Um, and you know, coming in as a rookie, um, you know, you want to be confident, you want to be, um, ready to learn, but you want to learn from the vets, you want to learn from the coaching staff. Um, and that's that's what I'm here to do. That's why I'm I'm going to steal knowledge from from everyone I can. I'm going to copy the vets that have done it right and have been been succeeding for years at this at this level. Um, and then, yeah, as far as like leadership, um, you know, just kind of continuing to be the guy that I that had built, you know, at Arizona. um you know if if I need to take up take up a leadership role obviously playing safety or kind of the quarterback of the defense like I'll be ready to step into that position because I've done it before. So >> talk about that leadership role. Uh yesterday I was talking to Daltton and he said that uh you took him under you know you took him under your wing and he said that you have like some old head tendencies and the way that you prepare your attention to detail kind of like what does that mean and kind of how do you think that that's rubbed off on him as a player? Yeah, I mean, uh, we we was trying to we was really coming up kind of around the same time, like I had gotten a little bit more snaps and then, you know, he started coming up in that spring and that's that's kind of when we really dove in together. Um, I think uh when he says oldhead tendencies, I think he just mean cuz I I don't do nothing like I just be at home and just watching tape and stuff. So, um, you know, he got we we just found a routine that worked for us. Um, and you know, we found ways to to keep getting better in all aspects of our game. So, um, yeah. No, it's been it's been super good for for both him and I, for sure. >> What's the biggest lesson you learned from the book, The Self-Centered Perspective? >> Um, that's my dad's book if if anyone's wondering. Um, I mean, honestly, like the best thing I took away is the acronym. Um, he's kind of, you know, turned it into a little program now. Um, just so it's heart. Um, so it's humility, efficacy, um, accountability, resilience, and trustworthiness. Um, I wear I wear it on my wrist every day. um just to remind myself those are, you know, the values I want to I want to show and and prove to myself every single day um in life and in football. Um so yeah, I think that's that's the main thing that's the main takeaway from that one for sure. >> Do you feel you got a lot of those lessons before you put them out to the world? >> Absolutely. Yeah. Um it's yeah it was it's funny you say that because like I read the book obviously in his voice and all I just it's just taking me back to being you know in fourth grade first year tackle football like the things he's telling me is the same things he's writing down. So um no but it was it was definitely cool to read it in a book and um uh realize that he's been teaching me that stuff my entire life. >> You obviously have a close relationship with Dalton, but you're coming in with two other uh rookie defensive backs in this draft class. What are your impressions of of Zeke and Germad so >> Yeah. Um really cool guys of course. Um I'm super excited u to have to to be able to play alongside both of them. Um Zeke look great. We got we got some good uh you know communication. Put some good tape together in this mini camp. Jam's making sure he's right. You know the training staff here is fantastic. So they're going to make sure he's good to go. Um and I'm super excited to get a chance to play with them. I think we're really going to do some good things for this organization. All right. Thanks. Thank you. Thank you guys. Go ahead. >> Questions for Trey, guys. Trey, >> one of the things that uh John Spek said about drafting you is that whoever you would just line up wherever you were lined up and just block who was ever in front of you. Like is that kind of just been your mentality throughout your football career? >> Pretty much. Yeah. Play wherever they need me. Play whatever gets me on the field and yeah, just block the guy in front of me. >> The communication with Fernando Mendoza, what's that been like? It's been great, you know, getting to know him, getting to talk with him, just off the field, on the field, working in the playbook. We had a little walk through last night, just kind of getting some snaps, getting some, you know, just time together. So, it's been great getting to know him. >> What's been your first impression of him just as a person off the field? >> He's just a guys guy, honestly. He just connects with everybody, super friendly, easy to talk to, you know, getting to know everybody. So, he's a great leader and I'm happy to be working with him. >> He talked about getting used to playing under center. He said that he was taking extra snaps with you guys at the hotel. What's that experience been like kind of helping him get used to that process? >> Right. Yeah, that's been awesome because yeah, we didn't do very much under center at&m either. So, it's been great, you know, getting those extra reps, you know, just texted and yeah, met at the hotel room last night and just, you know, got some extra reps under center. So, getting ready to roll. >> Is that cool kind of like bonding with him, you know, trying to learn something together kind of early on, >> right? Yeah, it's cool. Yeah. Just spending time with him, getting to know each other, you know, getting a connection with him. So, yeah, it's been awesome. >> There's so much talk about a quarterback learning to take snaps under center, but as you mentioned, center is same thing. like you have to adjust because you're doing a lot of shotgun. How different is that process to snap to somebody that's right behind you? >> I mean, it's a little different, but nothing that hasn't been too hard to pick up. You know, I've been working that the past couple months, you know, getting ready for this process, getting ready for the NFL. So, hasn't been too much difference. Just, you know, building that connection, you know, exactly how he likes it, cuz, you know, that's what matters. So, >> do you feel you could play all five positions at the NFL level? >> Yes, sir. 100%. How how much did you talk to teams about that throughout the process knowing like, you know, hey, I can do whatever you guys ask of me. I've showed it at the college level. Is that something that they talk to you when you talk to them about throughout this process? >> Yes, sir. Yeah, quite a bit because, yeah, I just want to get on the field as quick as possible, contribute to the team, help out the team, so wherever they need me, that's where I'm going to be. >> Where along the offensive line do you feel the most comfortable? >> Any of the five. I played mostly left tackle in college, but whatever they need, I'm comfortable playing. >> What are your first impressions of Rick Dennison? I love him as a coach. He's funny. He's fun to work with. You know, he's super detailed. I just love being in the meeting room with him and it's just a fantastic time getting to learn the playbook with him. >> Have you had any conversations with Linder Bomb yet? >> I have not. No, but I'm excited to. >> What are you excited to take away from him? >> I just want to be a sponge and learn everything I can. You know, he's he's a veteran guy. He knows what to do and just want to sit down with him and pick his brain. Hopefully not bug him too much, but just learn from him. What was the key to playing at the intensity level that you played at, but don't commit penalties? I think you only had one that was called on you last season, >> right? Yeah, it's just a mindset. Just being locked in, just being disciplined. You know, you got to do your job, but you got to do it right, too. So, it's just a mindset and something you got to work in practice every single day. >> So, Ricky CL as a whole so far, how able how have you guys been able to kind of juggle having fun and being high energy, but also being serious and treating this as it's a try out? >> I mean, yeah, that's it's just a job every single day. You got to come in, go to work, and then yeah, there's time, you know, when we're, you know, just sitting around in the hot tub, cold tub, you know, just, you know, messing around, talking around a little bit, just talking about other things. But, you know, when it's work time, it's work time, and everybody knows that. >> Versatility seem to be a key throughout the entirety of the draft class. How important is versatility, not only to yourself, but to everybody else on that's here in camp right now, >> right? It's super important. It's extremely important because, you know, being able to be versatile, play multiple positions just increases your value and how much you can help the team. So, it's all about what the team needs. So, you got to be able to help out however much you can. >> What's What do you feel is the most challen play all five positions? I I was wondering what's the most challenging part in terms of being able to do that at the high at a high level. >> Um, for mentally it wasn't really a problem because I pride myself on learning the playbook and learning all five positions, but you know, just getting those reps at all different positions because the technique is a little bit different, steps are a little bit different, just banking all those reps. So, just look forward to doing that in practice and on my own. You guys walked in with your name tags yesterday. Was there any like ice breakers you guys did to get to know each other off the field? >> I mean, just kind of talking in the locker room and then the O line room, you know, just, you know, favorite favorite foods, favorite uh musics, just kind of stuff like that. Just getting to know each other, getting to learn a couple things about each other. Can >> you talk about what the coaching styles of of Kubakino and Dennison have been so far and kind of what are the things that they're trying to instill in this offense? Uh, super hands-on. Um, very detailed. Extremely detailed. You know, you do it right and you do it until you do it right. So, yeah, extremely detailed and I'm just excited to continue to get to work with them. >> All good. >> Thank you. Cool. Appreciate y'all.

title: Cam Achord: ‘Attention to details’ is key to success on special teams
text: Just real quick, just give you a quick bio about myself and then we'll let you guys kind of open it up and start asking questions. Obviously, uh last two years been in New York um helping out there with the Giants. Prior to that was in New England, which you guys know. Um prior to that was junior college in Mississippi. Um which I fall back on a lot because when you're coaching a lot of different things, you got to focus on a lot of different things from doing the fields to equipment to every little ins and outs you can do. Um obviously born and raised in Mississippi. Um, spent my life 32 years there. Played caught small college ball in Jackson. Then I was blessed to get the opportunity to go to New England. So, real quick spill, you know, got a wife and a soon to be three-year-old. So, I know you guys want to get to doing football and everything, too. So, we'll let y'all open up with some questions and stuff. >> So, how how does a guy make the jump from junior college to the NFL? How does that happen? >> Yeah. Uh, relationships. So when I was at Southern Miss GA, my last year there, Joe Judge spent February to the end of March there, who's going to coach the tight ends and do special teams. So I got to know him there. So basically going in on the weekends from 6:00 a.m. to call it 10, 11:'clock at night just watching all this Alabama film because he just came from Alabama. Um, and then he got the call to go be Scotty O's assistant in New England. And so when he left, we just stayed in touch. um communicated. You know, I'd watch a lot more New England games then. Uh I go back to like the Super Bowl they played in. Um I take a picture of him talking to Bill on the sideline. You know, I send him a picture then like, "Hey, you're about to probably kick the onside kick, surprise on side kick there." Different things. Um but just communication and not really badgering the guy, but asking for advice here and there and just building a relationship. So to me, it doesn't matter whether you come in contact with somebody for 2 minutes or 5 minutes, you're going to make an impression on them. So, make sure you're making a good impression on somebody. Make sure they understand who you are and you're genuine. You'll hear me say that word a lot. Um, I believe in being genuine. I tell our guys to be genuine. Um, genuine excitement. You'll see me at practice once you get out there and stuff. I'll move around a pretty good bit. Um, but that that's really how I got there. He called me um asked me if I wanted to interview. Uh, so I went up there and actually interviewed. Bill wasn't there at the time, so I had to go back. I actually became the head coach of the junior college for about a month and a half during that time. Um, and I'm a very loyal person. So when Judge called me, he was like, "Hey, want to rein you? Bill wants to be here." And I was like, "I can't do it." You know, so I initially turned the second interview down, but about 4 hours later, I called him back and said, "Uh, what am I thinking?" So that's went up there, I got the interview, and Bill offered me the job that day. So that's how I ended up here. >> Cam, how much influence did you have on your team getting uh Trace Mack? >> You know, uh, it was a collaborative effort. you know, kind of like Goody Matt kind of allude to, you know, you give your opinion to those guys. You tell them where you kind of feel like guys are, where they where they will be, what what they'll be in the future. Um, to me, when you're projecting guys, you're not just projecting their first year. You're projecting what they can be in year two, three, four. Um, so you give your opinion to those guys, you say what you're convicted in, and then, you know, obviously that they make those decisions, but you're obviously giving your input. >> What about him stood out to you? >> Uh, straight ball, accuracy. Um, his ball doesn't move a lot. You know, for me, I don't need a guy, you know, and I've been blessed to coach a lot of guys that are really good. Um, I don't need a guy that can kick 65 yards personally. I want the guy that's going to put it through consistently from 58, 55 because again, we're playing in Green Bay, whether I was coaching New England, coaching at Met Life. We're going to play in elements and, you know, it's not you're not going to need the 60 yard ball all the time. You're going to need the 45 yard ball with a 14 mph crosswind. So, his ball not moving and stuff like that um was definitely a big part for me. >> How much of a of a thing is the Florida kicker learning how to kick in Green Bay? Is it is it is there more made of that than it should be? Or is that something that you do have to actually transition to the core when you're weather? >> For me personally, I think it's more made of than it is. I mean, just think about the history here, right? Ryan Longwell, Oregon, Cal, pretty good here, right? Mason Crosby, Texas, Colorado, pretty good here. I was blessed to coach Steven Guskowski. Mississippi, Memphis, New England, Nick Folk, California, Arizona, kick pretty good at Met Life, kicked pretty well. Um, so to me, I think it's a little bit more made up of the cold elements than there probably really is to it. Um, to me, it's more about their mindset and learning how to play their ball in the wind and the elements than it is actually the cold weather and those things. I mean, we're going to go kick cold football as a practice. We practice outside. So, um, we'll get used to that. You know, many times we can be outside or kick or be in Lambo and kick, the better we're going to be. >> The Giants were a good kickoff return team last year. What's the key to being successful under this current under this new format in terms of kickoff return? >> Uh, first first is buyin, you know, um, having guys that want to do it. Um, you know, that's the biggest thing and having a plan um, for those guys and and attacking it every day. You know, it's the little things. I tell the guys we're going to focus every day. It's the attention to details, just the can't win to you, keep from losing mindset. Don't commit penalties. Um, we're not going to want to start our offense inside the 30 yard line ever. You know, our goal is to get out past that. But it's each other knowing, understanding. Um, I tell the guys all the time, we want to consistently hit singles. Um, if you use a baseball analogy, you know, we're going to hit the singles, we're going to hit the singles, and then soon that pitcher's going to groove one, we're going to knock it out the park. So, it's the consistent thing, and it's doing those little things over and over and over. Um, but it starts with the fundamentals and the techniques. You'll hear me say that a good bit. Uh, it's the fundamentals. It's the hand placement. It's the blocking leverage. It's the returner knowing the tracks he has to run. Um, it's all tied together, but I think it's for our guys understanding the concept and then the belief in knowing, all right, as long as I do my job, it's going to set up everyone else out on the field. >> You were asked about Trey, but with deny Dennis Sutton having three block kicks in college, were you pounding the table, get this guy because he can help me, too? And what do you think of his skill set? Yeah. No, Den obviously had a very good skill set in college rushing punts, field goals, all that stuff. Um, I think any guy that's on our roster, we're going to put them in the position they do any skill set. Um, I think that's our job as coaches in general. What does the player do well and let's maximize that. What does he not do well and let's limit that. So, obviously he has some ability to block that showed up. Um, so that's something we'll definitely work on along with a bunch of other players on the roster for sure. What was this off seasonason like for you in terms of, >> you know, Rich leaves? I think it was five weeks after the season. What What was your plan at the time and how long were you talking to these guys, especially with the turnover in New York? >> Yeah, it obviously happened pretty fast. Um, you know, turnover in New York, so now you're on the phone as anyone else is. You're networking, you're calling, you're communicating. Um, you're talking to several people. I had I had a couple other options. I won't go into detail there. Um, potentially you should have respect for them. Uh but obviously when this opportunity came about and Matt called me, he goes, "Would you like to interview?" I said, "Yeah, absolutely. Would love to." Um and it was a pretty quick process um for me, you know, felt like it was an eternity. Um you know, but you know, went from go from the zoom to the in person to getting the job, you know, it's it was pretty quick. Um but I think the biggest thing was obviously being able to put you in a situation to be in touch with a guy. You know, I hadn't known Matt prior other than when we practiced here really when we practiced in 23 here. So >> for you to kind of go back to the kicking situation, have you ever been in a situation where you have three guys that are three quality guys like this and how much added I don't know stress pressure does it add on you as a coach to I guess make sure you have the right guy. >> I love it. More the marrier, you know, I mean brings me I've had as many as four so just to be honest. Uh so um they always have their strengths. They all have they're here for a reason, all of them. Um I think it's going to be a great competition. I think all those guys bring stuff to the table. So that's why they're all here. They're all professional football players. And we'll we'll work it. We'll manufacture where everybody's getting reps and we'll divide it up. But it's not something I'm new to um by any means. I mean, I honestly want to say my entire career. There's only been like one year that I've had actually maybe two, but every time if I've had two, don't quote me on that part, but I think it was two is the least amount I've ever had. Um kind of going into an offseason. We've always had at least two. Um most time it was three. I mean, the last two years in New York, we've had three the almost the whole year a lot of times. So, we'll work the reps accordingly for each of those guys and then working with, you know, Matt and Daniel off on side. >> What have you seen in Sky Moore's background and give you that he can get you those singles and doubles that you're looking for? >> Yeah. Um, obviously, you know, he was convicted running. Um, you know, and San Fran had a solid year. Um, he's done a lot of good things with the ball. You know, for me, returners, number one thing is holding on to the ball. We're not going to put it on the ground. um and being able to control the ball and catch the ball, right? Let's start there. We want to make sure we have the ball at the end of the play and then everything else. We'll talk about gaining the yards and everything, but you know, he was convicted. He's gotten better every year. I think if you go back to look at him where didn't do it in college, you know, then you see him, he gets to Kansas City, does it doesn't do then San Fran, he actually had a very productive year. So, I'm excited to work with him along with the other guys that are going to be back there. So, >> hey Cam, when you look at your time in New England there, you always hear from both Bill and Joe. you know, the emphasis they place on special teams, obviously the success they had in that area. What What do you think is the key to that? And just what did you take away, you know, from those years that that you did spent with those guys there? I >> I think it's the meticulous attention to the details is the number one and the fundamental techniques like it the kicking game is football. It's running, it's blocking, it's tackling, it's it's everything encompass um that you do on offense and defense. And I'll refer to offensive and defensive plays with our guys as much as I can, you know, um whether it's an outside zone play, whatever it may be, something that they register in their brain cuz they're coming from playing a lot of offense and defense in college most of the time. Um so just trying to relate to them that way and break it down and then maximizing your time on the things that are important, you know, and then it's the little things. Um hand placement, like I said, you know, how are your feet, how are you going to strike the guy in protections? um where is the where are they going to be at the communication aspect again nothing is going to get overlooked um you know that's big part I put our guys on is we'll do all the ground work y'all just show up and make sure you know kind of where we're at what we're going to do um in terms of aspects but I think it's the details is the biggest thing and making sure there is I don't like the philosophy of like not knowing whatifs um I like to think about that like all right well what if they did this what would we do trying to be proactive and having to answer before you go kind of into the battle, you know, on game day. >> It's been a long time since Greenbay's had good special teams, like positive units. How do you build a unit like mentality wise to get them to where you need them to get to? >> Yeah, I think it goes back to that initially like let's start with the fundamentals like I mean we go out to the field wherever we're going to start there. We're not getting a bunch of scheme. We got to do the little things right because then you lay the foundation, right? All right, we're going to lay a foundation and then we'll start maximizing that and it's putting the guys in a situation to be successful. Um, you know, I use the acronym with our guys is fax. I developed that in junior college. Um, because everybody I would talk to, they would be like, "Yeah, coach fax." You know, so I was like, "Okay, so it's focus with the right attitude to compete doing it together." So if we can do those four things every day, you know, we're going to end up having success on the field. It starts in the meeting room, starts the, you know, showing up with the right attitude, being genuine excited, you know, wanting to go to work, not, you know, having to be here. We get to go to work, you know, wanting to put the time in. And, you know, just having that rapport with the guys that they're excited to be out there on the field. And once you develop that and you develop the techniques, you know, I think everything else is going to take care of itself. >> Cam, you um you mentioned junior college a couple times. I don't know how accurate Wikipedia is. Was your last year there? Were you really the offensive coordinator, the special teams coordinator, the quarterback's coach, the running back's coach, and the tight end's coach, >> and the recruiting coordinator if you want to add it on there. But, uh, yes, I was. Yeah. So, we had on offensive staff, we had the O line coach, um, who actually was the, uh, you know, we had the O line coach, and then we had one other coach, myself, we're really coaching the entire offense, and then I did the special teams. So, that's kind of where I developed the not sleeping habit, I think. you know. >> So, so like they and they've got a guy to worry about the lights and the and the turf getting mowed and everything else. >> But, so how does that how does that time influence you? It's been a long time since you did that, but I'm guessing those formative years were pretty important. >> They were very important to me. Um, I tell everybody I think some of the best coaches are people that coach small college ball, you know, whether that's division 2, division 3, junior college, because you have to wear a lot of hats. And so it makes you put the stuff that's really important in a bucket and let's get take care of that, the stuff that maybe is not so important. Everything's important, but there's obviously levels to everything. Um, but it also makes you maximize your time. You know, when you're doing all those different things, it's you've got to lay out a day. You've got to be organized. So that really helped me with the organization process because not only were you scripting for the offense, then you had to turn around script for special teams practice, then you had to let the other coaches know where to go, what to do, what part, because you had to use everybody as a coach obviously during the drills. Um, so I say you helped me develop into a lot better coach, you know, and and I rely back on a lot. >> And thanks to New England, you're undefeated as a head coach then. >> That's correct. That's right. I don't know with the way that things laid out, it was late in the hiring process for the coaching carousel. Did I don't know if you saw this job had opened before you heard from Matt, but when you saw that there was a coordinator job open so late like what what was your initial reaction to that? And were you just kind of like chomping for a a chance to to get back into this type of role? >> Yeah, I I think the initial reaction is like, you know, is it a job you want? I I don't think I think there's jobs out there that you may or may not want all the time. It's like what's the situation? Um can you be successful in that situation? Um there's always you don't want to make impulse decisions, you know, you want to take a second um take a breath. Um but obviously once you know you take that breath, it's like what is it? And obviously this is a historic franchise team. It's a very unique team as well. obviously being one of one um in the situation, but I was obviously excited to get the phone call. You know, I think it is a great opportunity. Um I would say like for me it's an opportunity that I wanted again to be a coordinator as well. Um you know, just was blessed to get the opportunity from Matt and then obviously, you know, get the opportunity to be here. >> In terms of of seeing it as a job where you could be successful at, what what was it that made this job attractive to you? Yeah, I mean I think there's pieces in place. I think there's players here. I think Matt understands that uh the kicking game he's been great for me um already, you know, so I think it's, you know, just there's an opportunity here to improve and get better and um just there there's already pieces here, you know, you're not going into a situation where you're like, "Oh man, we're definitely starting from scratch with everything." Um, I mean there was obviously a lot of, you know, toughness already about the team and stuff like that. So just there was just a little bit of things when you looked at it like obviously Daniel was Daniel, those type of things, but there's just enough pieces you're like, "Hey, we have an opportunity to be successful in the kicking game." >> Dan, with Daniel, Cam, what what stands out to you about him and where do you kind of see his arrow, you know, pointing as a punter? >> Yeah. Um, obviously he had a tremendous year last year. Um, we've sat down, we've talked. Um, you know, I tell the guys, we're either getting better or we're getting worse. You know, you're never going to really stay the same. So, our goal is every day to get better. Um, and and he's attacking it that way. He's been great so far. Obviously, limited interaction with him. Um, so we'll continue to get better, but, you know, we'll see where it goes. >> Do you still drink six cups of coffee and three Pepsis every day? >> No, I've cut back, you know. Um, I still have a lot. Uh, not that many. I tried to I tried to cut back. I would say now I'm down to about 3 to four and I've cut out the calf uh sodas really. So I'm probably down to three or four coffees. Two before and then maybe one or two after about 2:00 I'll have one every day. Um but I'm naturally a high energy person anyway. I don't need it. So you know we'll see.
